text: The assembly will now hear an address by
His Excellency
Gemang,
President of the Swiss Confederation. I
request protocol to escort his
excellency and invite him to address the
assembly.
President,
>> President of the General Assembly,
United Nations Secretary General, Heads
of State and Government, Your
Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen.
Switzerland is a country of mountains,
valleys, and different languages. Part
of our history, therefore, meant
learning to live with what divides us.
We didn't make the mountains disappear.
First, we learned to climb them, then to
cross them.
To do so, we built roads, bridges, and
tunnels. And we realized that a natural
boundary is not necessarily a dividing
line. It can also be a pathway that
connects us.
This very simple experience seems to me
to have something to teach us about the
world in which we live because we are
going through a time of upheaval. The
international order established in the
aftermath of the Second World War is
under severe constraints. Conflicts are
multiplying and becoming deadlocked. The
most fundamental principles of the
United Nations Charter, the prohibition
of the use of force and respect for
sovereignty and territorial integrity
are being openly violated.
Added to this are transformations that
are reshaping our societies. climate
change and the increase in the number of
disasters, humanitarian crises,
inequalities,
and also technological upheavalss,
notably artificial intelligence, which
are often advancing faster than our
collective ability to assess their
implications.
At the same time, multilateral
institutions are having to respond to an
increasing number of crises while facing
pre pressure on resources and an erosion
of trust. The theme of this 81st session
of the General Assembly, restoring
trust, managing transformation, a united
nations that delivers for all, therefore
aptly sums up the task before us
to restore trust.
To support transformation and to
demonstrate through concrete results
that cooperation remains possible. This
erosion of trust extends far beyond the
realms of peace and security.
We're also seeing it in the global
economy. Protectionism is on the rise.
Supply chains built up over decades of
interdependence
are being reorganized or fragmented as a
result of geopolitical tensions.
The multilateral trading system has been
weakened
and the WTO can no longer fully carry
out some of its essential functions.
Yet what is at stake here is not merely
a technical issue of trade policy.
The question is whether relations
between states
will continue to be governed by common
rules or if they will increasingly
depend on the weight and power of each
individual state. For Switzerland, this
is a fundamental issue. That is because
my country is an open economy with few
natural resources.
A large part of its prosperity therefore
depends on trade, but also on the
stability and predictability of the
rules that make such trade possible.
Economic resilience requires us to
diversify relationships, forge new
partnerships, and keep trade between
different regions of the world as open
as possible.
This is particularly important for
economies with fewer resources
or limited market access.
Access to markets, knowledge, and
technology can create opportunities that
would not otherwise exist.
These abstract concepts encompass quite
concrete realities. A business that can
take on an apprentice, a family that can
secure a more stable income,
a producer who can trade beyond their
local market, young people for whom the
range of possibilities suddenly widens.
That is also what we mean when we talk
about a global economy.
Trust is built when the rules offer
everyone a genuine opportunity to
participate. It is also built when
states continue to engage in dialogue.
Switzerland is neutral. This neutrality
goes handinhand with a steadfast
commitment to the UN charter,
international law, and the UN's three
pillars, peace and security,
human rights, and sustainable
development. Our experience has also
taught us that dialogue is not a sign of
weakness. Engaging in dialogue does not
mean glossing over disagreements or
abandoning one's principles. Engaging in
dialogue means maintaining contact when
positions begin to diverge.
A bridge does not require the two banks
of a river to become alike. It simply
allows us to cross from one to the
other. In times of tension, this
possibility often becomes essential.
Dialogue is a tool for deescalation.
when crises erupt. Above all, it can
serve as a means of prevention before
crisis arise.
It is in this spirit that Switzerland
will continue to offer its good offices
and provide spaces where those who are
no longer on speaking terms can when
when circumstances permit resume
dialogue.
Geneva is one sh such space. It is home
to the UN, the WTO, and numerous other
international organizations, as well as
scientific ones, humanitarian actors,
representatives of civil society, and
permanent missions of almost every
country in the world. Every day, people
from different backgrounds, representing
interests that are sometimes at odds
with one another, come together here.
They do not need to agree in order to
talk to one another. That is exactly
what gives such a place its value.
Switzerland will therefore continue as
the host state to ensure that Geneva
remains open, accessible, and inclusive
for large states and small for the north
and the south. But inclusion is not
merely about having a seat at the table.
It also means being able to make a real
contribution to decisions that will
affect one's own future.
This is the case with international
cooperation.
Every society must be able to shape its
future in accordance with its history,
needs, and priorities.
Cooperation is not about imposing one's
own values or a single model. It is
valuable when it creates partnerships,
facilitates the sharing of expertise,
and strengthens everyone's capacity to
act independently.
It is less about doing things for others
than doing things with them.
This principle takes on particular
significance in the face of current
technological revolutions.
AI is the most obvious illustration of
this. It offers considerable new
possibilities in science, the economy,
medicine, education, and the management
of resources.
But it also highlights the risk of a new
divide between those who have the skills
and infrastructure needed to participate
in this transformation and those who are
likely to feel only its effects. We must
ensure that technological progress
broadens opportunities without widening
the gaps. This means that as many
countries and societies as possible
must be able to benefit from advances in
AI,
develop their skills and contribute to
the debate on the rules that will govern
its development and use.
This is exactly the aim of the Geneva AI
summit which will take place on the 21st
and 22nd of June 2027 under the motto
bridging innovation and trust.
These two concepts must go hand in hand.
Innovation in which societies no longer
have confidence risks being rejected.
Conversely, rules that would prevent all
innovation would deprive us of enormous
potential.
Our responsibility therefore is to
strike a balance to enable progress and
promote its benefits while creating the
conditions for the reliable and
responsible development and use of these
technologies.
Artificial intelligence thus reminds us
of a simple truth. Certain changes are
so far reaching and so fast moving that
no single state can manage all of their
consequences by itself. We need
institutions capable of dealing with
issues that transcend national borders.
We need multilateralism.
But multilateralism will only retain its
credibility if it is also able to
evolve. Switzerland therefore supports
efforts to reform the UN system as part
of the UN80 initiative. This reform must
make the UN more coherent, more
effective, and more resultsoriented
while respecting the powers and
responsibilities of member states.
The UN must focus its efforts where its
action brings real added value when
problems transcend borders when national
or regional capacities are insufficient
or when a universal institution is
needed to provide a common framework.
The key question is therefore a simple
one. How can we ensure that the
resources, expertise, and energy
invested in the multilateral system
yield better results for those it is
meant to serve.
Because our institutions do not exist
for their own sake. They exist for the
people, for those who live in fear of
conflict, for those who have lost their
home following a disaster, for those
seeking work or building a future for
themselves, for the children whose lives
depend on access to education. and the
new opportunities we are creating today.
It is on this scale that the value of
multilateralism is ultimately measured.
Ladies and gentlemen, your excellencies,
we cannot make the diverging interests
of our countries disappear. We cannot
erase disagreements, rivalries, or
borders. Nor can we remove all of the
mountains that stand between us. But we
can determine how we wish to tackle
them.
We can preserve open dialogue rather
than erect more barriers. We can keep
the channels of communication open
rather than resigning ourselves to
silence. We can ensure that
technological progress creates more
opportunities rather than new divisions.
And we can reform our institutions
rather than accept their gradual demise.
Switzerland will continue to play its
part using the means at its disposal by
upholding international law, promoting
dialogue, providing its good offices,
supporting effective multilateral
institutions,
and by remaining a country where the
world can continue to come together and
engage.
We do not claim to have all the answers,
but our experience in the Alps has
taught us one simple thing. While a
mountain might separate us, it can just
as easily be crossed.
Crossing it brings people together.
Coming together encourages dialogue, and
dialogue fosters trust.
Perhaps this is where our shared
responsibility begins to keep open the
pathways that allow us in spite of our
differences to continue moving forward
hand in hand. Thank you very much for
your attention.
On behalf of the assembly, I wish to
thank the president of the Swiss
Confederation.
